definition: A set of memory optimization techniques for distributed training that eliminates redundant storage of optimizer states, gradients, and parameters across data-parallel workers.
details: ZeRO enables training much larger models than would otherwise fit in available GPU memory by partitioning (rather than replicating) optimizer state, gradients, and parameters across the devices participating in data-parallel training.

explainer.lead: ZeRO cuts the memory each data-parallel worker must hold by partitioning optimizer states, gradients, and parameters instead of replicating them. That lets teams train models far larger than any single GPU's memory would allow.

tiers.eli5: Like splitting a huge shared textbook across classmates so each person carries only a few chapters instead of a full copy, then swapping pages when needed.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers apply ZeRO stages to shrink per-GPU memory during large-scale data-parallel training. A pitfall is the added communication from gathering partitioned pieces, which can slow training if not tuned.
tiers.paperLevel: Instead of replicating optimizer states, gradients, and parameters on every data-parallel device, these tensors are partitioned across devices; partitioning rather than replicating is what removes redundancy.

explainer.example: A model whose full optimizer state, gradients, and parameters would not fit in one GPU's memory is trained by splitting those tensors across the data-parallel workers.

citation.title: ZeRO: Memory Optimizations Toward Training Trillion Parameter Models
